title: Build an AI adoption scorecard for your team
description: A system that scores your team's real AI usage against the story you're telling yourself about it.

push.title: Push
push.content: Sending your local commits up to GitHub so the online repo matches your computer. When Claude says it's 'pushing to GitHub,' it's uploading your latest changes so they're saved in the cloud and visible to others.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

action.title: Action
action.content: A step an automation performs after the trigger fires — like 'send a Slack message' or 'create a Notion page.' One workflow can chain a dozen actions off a single trigger.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Most adoption stories are aspirational. Gartner's HR leader survey found that 88% of organizations have not realized significant business value from AI tools, per [Gartner's survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-10-28-gartner-survey-shows-88-percent-of-hr-leaders-say-their-organizations-have-not-realized-significant-business-value-from-ai-tools). This system pulls usage signals, training completion, tool access, and informal feedback into a scorecard you run every quarter, so you find out whether your team is the exception or part of that majority.

Leadership support is the sharpest predictor change-management research has found. Organizations with smooth AI rollouts score leadership's own visible use at +1.65 on a -2 to +2 scale, struggling ones at -1.50, per [Prosci's research](https://www.prosci.com/ai-change-management). The scorecard should measure your own visible usage too.

Run it as a quarterly paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt), a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill), or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that pulls straight from your team's usage logs. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) against the underlying data.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming the signals you can realistically gather, your scoring rubric, your cadence, and who sees the results.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that scores my team's actual AI adoption, not the story we tell ourselves about it. Ask me questions, one at a time, about what signals I can realistically gather (usage data, training records, survey responses, informal feedback), how often I want to run this, what a passing versus failing score looks like for my team, and who should see the results. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming what you can gather up front keeps the scorecard honest instead of aspirational.

items: What usage data you can access without invading anyone's privacy.
Whether the survey component is anonymous, and how that changes what people admit.
How often the scorecard reruns and who sees the trend line over time.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather what it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are your AI tool's admin console for usage logs, your training platform for completion records, and a survey tool for the trust layer. The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on whatever data you have on hand. The prompt below is an example of the core task. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Score my team's AI adoption across trust, training, tools, and actual usage, using the data I give you.

Context: Here's what I have: [usage logs, training completion records, a short anonymous survey, tool license data]. My team is [size/function].

Rules:
- Score each of the four dimensions (trust, training, tools, usage) separately. Don't average them into one number that hides where the real gap is.
- Cite the specific evidence behind each score. Don't just assert a level.
- If a dimension has no real data behind it, say "unmeasured," don't guess.
- Recommend the single highest-impact next step, not a long list.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: scoring each dimension separately stops a strong tools score from masking a weak trust score.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Each dimension scored on its own, evidence cited, gaps marked unmeasured instead of guessed?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what went wrong ("the usage log is three months stale, weight it lower") and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Run it before and after a training [push](#tooltip-push) to measure impact.
Break scores out by team or function to find where the gap really sits.
Make your own visible usage public alongside your team's.
Turn the lowest-scoring dimension into next quarter's one focused intervention.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each scorecard, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for quarter, score per dimension, evidence cited, biggest gap found, and action taken. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log makes it obvious whether last quarter's [action](#tooltip-action) moved a score at all.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. After a year of quarters it shows whether the intervention you picked moved the score, or just felt productive. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a couple quarters straight, package the prompt, the scoring rules, and the log format into a reusable AI skill. A check that fails again and again is a candidate for a skill of its own. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. A scorecard that only measures what's easy to measure, license counts, misses the real gap, which usually sits in trust and training.
